title: Rabies Requires Quarantine; Dog-Trade Claims Require Proof
excerpt: Rabies can kill after symptoms begin. Dog-trade defenses cannot replace quarantine, traceability, or proof of lawful sourcing. Vietnam needs abolition by 2030.
body_html:
One fact should cut through every defense of the dog-meat trade: once rabies symptoms appear, disease is virtually 100% fatal. Exposure demands immediate wound washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, followed by urgent medical assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis when indicated. World Health Organization guidance leaves no room for delay.

Tradition cannot replace traceability

“Farm-raised” is a claim, not proof. Lawful sourcing requires records, animal identification, veterinary oversight, transport controls, and quarantine compliance. Without those records, no reader can know whether an animal came from a licensed source, crossed checkpoints without inspection, or was taken from a family. Pet theft allegations demand police records and court judgments. They must be investigated, not dismissed—and never inflated with unsupported stories.

Public safety needs more than household caution

Household rabies exposure and commercial supply-chain risk are separate dimensions of broken biosecurity. A bite, scratch, or infected saliva entering broken skin or mucous membranes can transmit rabies. Handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and uncontrolled transport create preventable risk. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Safe communities need vaccination, quarantine, enforcement, and transparent supply chains.

Vietnamese communities can set the standard

Families, veterinarians, local officials, and animal-protection leaders can reject illicit operators who profit from stolen companions and unsafe movement. Government rabies-control targets are not the same as SDE’s policy demand: complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030.

Sign the national petition calling for nationwide abolition by 2030. Add your name to a public demand for action, then follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers.

• Possible exposure requires wound washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, then urgent medical assessment.
• Vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies may be needed before symptoms develop.
• “Farm-raised” claims cannot replace animal records, quarantine, transport controls, or proof of lawful sourcing.
• Household exposure and commercial supply-chain risk are separate biosecurity failures. Neither supports complacency.
• Pet theft claims need police and court records. Illicit operators must face investigation, not protection through vague tradition claims.

Vietnamese families, veterinarians, officials, and community leaders can demand traceability now—and complete abolition by 2030.

Rabies control cannot stop at household gates. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After a possible exposure, people must wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care. Vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies must come before symptoms develop.

This public-health reality makes loose dog-trade claims unacceptable. “Farm-raised” is not proof. Lawful sourcing requires records, animal identification, veterinary oversight, transport controls, and quarantine compliance. Without those safeguards, communities cannot verify where animals came from or whether family pets entered illicit supply chains. Pet-theft allegations must receive serious police and court investigation. No one should protect criminal operators with vague appeals to tradition.

Vietnamese families, veterinarians, local officials, and animal-protection leaders can demand stronger enforcement and transparent records. Household rabies exposure and commercial trade risk are separate problems, but both show why biosecurity cannot depend on trust alone.
